utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And good afternoon to everyone, and welcome back after our extended weekend. The -- we have been alerted -- Mr. Hannis, you seem to be about to rise. We have been alerted that the witness has something to say, and we intended to deal with that first. But do you have a matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was only rising in anticipating of announcing the appearances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the appearances. Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith for the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Melody Whittaker appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, the -- as I said, we have been alerted that the witness wishes to say something. So unless there are some preliminary matters that we should deal with before that, I propose to have the witness brought into the stand to see what -- what he wishes to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Welcome back. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. We are given to understand that there -- that before we resume your examination-in-chief and -- there is something that you wish to say to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. First of all, I would like to greet everybody present, and I'll bring forward the matter immediately. The reason why I'm taking the floor is the article that was published on SENSE Tribunal. The article is biased, but I'll -- I don't want to go into that. It, however, concerns also some lies. And before we continue, let me ask you if you can do anything about it. And I can say to you what is wrong there. I don't know how this works anyway. Is there a -- a PR representative here, or is the press present during the trials, or how does everything work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. We have, indeed, seen the article in SENSE, and we're also somewhat surprised to learn of the contents. However, we find that it would be inappropriate for the Court itself to address any journalist or newspaper every time something wrong is written about this Tribunal, so this is normally taken care of by the Registry, in which there is a Press and Information Section which normally deals with foreign press relations. So I assume that the Press and Information Section has already sought to clear up the -- the wrongful information that appeared in Sense. But we can check that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Judge Harhoff addressing the witness's legitimate concerns. And if there is nothing else, I, sir, would remind you that you're still on your oath and invite Mr. Hannis to conclude his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just indicate that I wasn't aware of the article, I haven't seen the article myself. The witness may want to speak to Victim Witness to see if there's a way that maybe he can speak directly with people from SENSE. I don't know what the issue is, but that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With that, I have about, I think, five or ten minutes, Mr. Planojevic, and then Mr. Zecevic will have his turn. I just want to establish the number of times and the chronology on -- regarding the occasions that official representatives have spoken with you about some of the events from 1992. We've already talked about your interview with OTP in June of 1992 -- or in June of 2004, I'm sorry. Do you recall having given a statement or a deposition in November of 2004 - I think it was the 23rd of November, 2004 - in connection with an investigation that was being done by the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina concerning the deaths of three Muslim families in September of 1992? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, but could we have the date when this -- when this last document was disclosed to the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's -- it's contained within Exhibit P1543, which is the document from the regional prosecutor. And the witness's statement is at page -- begins at page 47 of the English in e-court, and I think it's page 41 of the B/C/S in e-court. I'm only asking to confirm the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis, but wasn't it agreed between the parties that we would be notified that you want to use another document which is not on your list previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As far as I'm -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm not -- and I'm not concerned that -- I'm not aware that it was on your list. I might be mistaken, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I'm sorry, it's tab 21. I withdraw. I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, all I want to ask right now is if you remember having given that deposition?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't given to the OTP. I gave that statement to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. I think it was the police that were taking the statement or the deposition on behalf of the public prosecutor's office. Do you recall having met with other representatives of the OTP in February of 2009, Ms. Joanna Korner and Jusu Yarmah?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at Nedzarici, near Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it was near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then in May of this year, on May the 12th, in Bijeljina, a meeting with a Mr. Paul Grady and Belinda Pidwell and an interpreter from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about your contacts with Mico Stanisic after -- after the war. And I guess I will ask you: Did you have any contacts with Mico Stanisic after the year 2004, after you had your first interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had one contact with him in Belgrade. But I'm not sure whether it was before or after that date. It was probably after.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In -- in speaking with Ms. Korner and Mr. Yarmah in 2009 you informed them that you had had a contact from Mr. Stanisic about the possibility of being a witness for him regarding events before the war, and at that time I think you said it had been a couple of months earlier, so maybe the end of 2008; does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That contact must have taken place much earlier. I'm not sure now because it's been a long time, but I did say to him that I had had that contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that a face-to-face meeting, or by phone, or ... or what?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was face to face.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you in that meeting that he had read your 2004 interview?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, really not. We -- we spoke a little, and I -- actually, I volunteered the information. I spoke about the circumstances of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that in the brief witness statement that Ms. Korner and Mr. Yarmah took from you on the 24th of February, 2009, it was reported that Mico Stanisic, you said, in paragraph 6, "He told me that he had read my statement which I gave in Banja Luka in 2004," would that refresh your memory, or do you disagree with that now?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said as much to them, but Mico said that he knew what I had said. That's the crux of the matter. But there may be a discrepancy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. We were talking last time you were here about Zoran Jasarevic and Goran Abazovic, two of the men who provided personal security for --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abazovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Abazovic -- who provided personal security for the minister in 1992. In 1992, do you recall what they wore? Did they wear civilian clothes, did they wear a uniform? What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abazovic was in uniform, and I think that Jasarevic was in civilian clothes. Actually, I only saw him two or three times. I'm really not sure about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Abazovic's uniform, can you tell us what colour it was, what type it was, was it a camouflage uniform; and, if so, what colour?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the basic colours, was it a forest camouflage green; was it blue camouflage; or some other colour?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, forest green, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now the Malovic Unit, we've heard evidence from some witnesses that they had a distinctive kind of camouflage. Do you recall the uniforms that they wore?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had various kinds of uniforms. I don't know which you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that their camouflage uniform was somewhat distinctive from the normal blue camouflage or green camouflage that most others were wearing at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had both blue camouflage and glean camouflage, I think. But when they arrived at Vraca, and that's probably what you were interested in, they had black and white. But only for a very brief period. They probably understood that those uniforms were unsuitable for combat. So after a month, I never saw them in such uniforms again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see them in other kinds of uniforms after that month, or did you see them at all?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that they held the line behind the school where we basically lived for a month and a half or two. And they would come to lunch often, and we would meet them there. I know I saw them there in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you moved from Vraca to Pale, I think you said that was in June of 1992, early June. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you work, where was your office located in Pale? What building or hotel or ...

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was at Kalovita Brda. Before the war, it was a scouts centre, or dorm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that facility?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I resigned. But I did come by even later, informally or unofficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where Mico Stanisic's office was located in June and July and the rest of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I remember such a contact at hotel -- at the Kosuta hotel. I believe that his office was up there, but I'm not sure. It may have been at the Bistrica hotel because part of the cabinet was there too. But I met the then-minister at the Kosuta hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned the government, Mr. Djeric. Do you know where his offices were in June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Bistrica hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I think you told us that you started working for the national security in September of 1992; is that -- is that about right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was your office when you started working for them, until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same building. Until October or November, when we went to Bijeljina. The headquarters moved then. Part of the service left a bit earlier, two or three men, to -- they went to look for accommodation. And I think that we followed in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say your office was in the same building, you mean in Kalovita Brda?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Bijeljina, when you got there, where was your office? Was it in the SJB building or the CSB building? Are those two different buildings; and, if so, which one were you in?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were accommodated at the CSB, and the ministry moved to the same building. Even now, it's the services centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was the minister housed in Bijeljina in late 1992; and, if so, where was his office?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can believe me that I never saw the minister in Bijeljina, either in that period or later. I believe another man was in charge of affairs there, one or two men. It may seem ridiculous, but that was really the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who are the one or two men that you're referring to in that context?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cedo Kljajic, when we arrived. But only very briefly. And then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Kijac was in charge of state security. And I think that Tovo [as interpreted] Kovac, as the chief of the police, or the [indiscernible] service, took care of these affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Planojevic. Those are all of the questions I have for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Planojevic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On Friday we had some problems with your fast speech, so I will ask you to speak slowly to enable the interpreters to interpret both my question and your answer. On Friday, you -- the -- your -- the statement was given to you that you made on the 8th and 9th of June, 2004. You had it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you still have it, or did you return it to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- I left it in my suitcase in my room. It's here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll remind you of some parts of that interview which you discussed with my learned friend on Friday and at the beginning of this hearing. You gave this interview to the OTP's investigators, among whom there was a lawyer of the OTP, and you did so on the 8th and 9th of June, 2004, in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you were interviewed as a suspect, and you were told as much; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's mentioned in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But it's true, isn't it, that until three days before you gave that interview, that is, round about the 5th of June, you were the acting chief inspector of the State Security Service, or the intelligence agency as it was called then, which service used to exist on the 5th of June so that when you were giving that interview, you were a ministry employee without a particular task or position; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, please just wait for a couple of seconds after my question and then answer, for the sake of the interpreters. At that moment, you didn't have a post when you were invited to come and talk to the OTP representatives. They told you that they were interviewing you as a suspect and then they read out to you the definition of the notion of "suspect." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, on page 1 of the transcript of this interview, it says that a suspect is a person concerning whom the Prosecution has reliable information indicating that there is a possibility that that person has committed a crime which falls under the jurisdiction of the International Tribunal. Do you remember this being said to you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, the OTP investigators also advised about your rights, including that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry to interrupt, but my English translation of what was read out to him on page 1 is: "The definition of a suspect is a person concerning whom the Prosecution possesses reliable information which tends to show that the persons may have committed a crime." And I don't see "may have" in what was appearing in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree. I see that this was omitted. I said that indicating that there is a possibility that the person has committed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we do not have the original text, so we're doing simultaneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For purposes of the interpreter, this is 65 ter 9106. And I have a hard copy in B/C/S for the witness, if that will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 9106 in e-court. And could the witness be given a hard copy in the Serbian language; that would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would alert my friend that unfortunately the English page and the B/C/S page don't exactly much up, as is usually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As usual is the case, I will have to deal with that. Thank you. [Interpretation] Could we now go to page 2, please, of this document, both -- in both versions. And I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutors of the OTP advised you of your rights that, among others, you have a right to have a lawyer present during the interview; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, you have been a professional policeman since 1973; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your career with the police, and it was a continuous career that went on for 31 years, if I understood it right, and during that time, you completed all police schools that existed within the former SFRY, including the university in Skoplje; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't want you to misunderstand me but you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that you belonged to the old police school? I'm not criticizing you; this is by no means intended as a criticism. Rather, I just want to inform the Chamber, acquaint the Chamber, with the context. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it had a positive connotation in our system when one said that one belonged to the old police system, old police school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you. And in my mind it also has a positive ring to it. Now tell me, please, it's true, isn't it, that this connotation of the old classic-type police school had a rather cautious attitude or suspicious attitude toward those suspects who asked for a lawyer to be present during interview?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As you were taught in the former Yugoslavia, if somebody was innocent, then that person didn't need a lawyer; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Because it wasn't really customary in our system to have lawyers present when somebody was interviewed. It just wasn't something that was widespread in practice, until the changes. And when I say "changes," I mean the changes that came with the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you. Our Law on Criminal Procedure did not envisage mandatory presence of counsel in pre-indictment proceedings; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, according to that old police school to which you belonged, as soon as somebody asked for a lawyer to be present or asked for legal assistance, that was a signal to you that there were some elements of criminal responsibility present with respect to that person?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sure that you will agree with me that, among other things, that was also the reason why you did not ask for a lawyer to be present when you were interviewed in 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And I -- and if I can give you a clarification for additional reason or you will come to that yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be more efficient, let me put questions to you. And if I miss something, you will be given an opportunity to add what you need to say at the end. Will that work?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This interview that you had on the 8th and 9th of June, 2004, was recorded; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The investigators of the OTP told you that at the conclusion of the interview you would be given a copy of tapes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on page 3 of this interview, they also said to you, in paragraph 1, that -- they said to you that should you become no longer a suspect but an accused, then the transcripts of the tape that was recorded would be made; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And we see that the transcript was subsequently made. When did you learn that the transcript had been made?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the interview in Bijeljina. I don't know the date, but that was the last time I talked to the OTP. In the evening, at 8.00 p.m., the interpreter brought the transcript to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that that was the meeting you had with the representatives of the OTP in May of this year; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And since this was brought to your house at 8.00 p.m., you were supposed to show up in the morning for that meeting at what time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it is recorded in the document. I was supposed to come at 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you were expected to go over the transcript from 8.00 p.m. until the meeting in the morning. And the transcript contains, as far as I know, about 150 pages; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you will agree with me, won't you, that, essentially, the first opportunity you had to read in detail the transcript of your interview given on the 8th and 9th of June, 2004, only here, when you came to The Hague last week; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is then that I started thinking about the actual meaning of each and every word and sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I said "in detail," that's precisely what I had in mind. And if I understood your evidence on Friday well, you immediately informed the OTP, as soon as you met with them on the 19th, in the morning -- you told them that you had certain amendments and interventions in relation to this transcript. Also, if I understood your evidence on Friday well, the Prosecutor got somewhat angry; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now go back to this 2004 interview. It is a fact, isn't it, and this is somewhat [as interpreted] that was put to you by the Prosecutor on Friday, that in 2004 the investigators of the OTP in the presence of one counsel of the OTP told you that you were not the target of the investigation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something along those lines. Something to that effect was said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will read it now. It is the last sentence on page 3. Nicolas Sebire, the investigator of the OTP, says as follows: "Since, during this interview, you had status of a suspect, before we start the questioning I would like to inform you that you are not the target of our investigation. Do you understand that?" That's what was said to you, and you answered that you understood it.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, on Friday, when you answered the questions of Mr. Hannis, even though back in 2004 you said you understood it, on Friday you said that that wasn't entirely clear to you what that meant, to have the status of a suspect without being the target of the investigation. Do you remember saying this in evidence?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you were told that you were a suspect and when the definition of the term "suspect" was read out to you, which said that the Prosecution had reliable information indicating that that person may have committed a crime from the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, when one translated this into our legal system, that meant that somebody -- that there were reasons to suspect, that there were grounds to suspect, that ... you committed a crime. And this is how you understood your status; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Even when you were told that you were not the target of the investigation, you could rationally conclude that even though you had the status of a suspect, you could have been suspected of being an accomplice or a co-perpetrator of the person against whom the investigation was conducted; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, I'm sure that did you not feel comfortable in that situation; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the least comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you served as a professional policeman for 31 years, had you ever been in a situation where you were interviewed as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what I'm particularly interested is, is something you said on Friday, page 16442 of the transcript. You said, among other things, in your answer, that when somebody sent you a message to the effect that you had to be cooperative or else you would be fired, and this something you mentioned in the context of your interview with the Prosecutor, when you received this message, I would like to know whether this message was conveyed to you by an investigator or the OTP counsel or somebody else. And I'm not really interested in the name or other details of the person sending you the message.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was given to me indirectly, and it could have been conveyed by the lawyer -- was Trivun a lawyer? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you were interviewed, there were five of you all together. There were two investigators of the OTP; there was Julian Nicholls, counsel of the OTP; there was the interpreter; and you. Those are the people who were there in June.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, this message that you should be cooperative or else you would be fired was not conveyed to you by any of the three persons from the OTP, neither the investigators, nor Mr. Julian Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this warning, if I may call it that, was conveyed to you by another person; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did you receive this warning? How long before the interview held on the 8th and 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps five to six days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it was then, precisely, that you were given notice that you would be interviewed by the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Planojevic, did you have any reason to doubt that should you be non-cooperative when talking to the OTP investigators you would not be fired?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was always present, because such things were known to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, that you really did retire some six months after that, in 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to another topic. You say in the interview, and I believe you repeated it on Friday in this courtroom, and I mean the interview given on the 8th, that you were a member of the Communist party, that is, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia before 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is also a fact - and you spoke about that on Friday, I believe - that on one occasion the newly appointed minister, after the elections on the victory of the ethnic parties, you were in charge of an operation when the minister was deprived of liberty; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was not me. It was one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said. You didn't understand. You were involved in an investigation in which Alija Delimustafic was targeted, among others, and he was placed in a remand prison for about 30 days; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I signed the order to conduct that investigation, and that's how it was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure I won't be wrong when I say that you did not exactly enjoy the trust of those ethnic parties; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yeah, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You related an incident to us when you got a job at Marin Dvor, which is a significantly lower-ranking position than your previous one and was not in line with your qualifications. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then you tried to contact Mr. Zepinic, who was the highest-ranking Serb official in the MUP and who was in charge of Serb personnel in the MUP, but he never got back to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you contacted -- or, rather, went to see Mr. Momo Mandic, who, in terms of rank, was the second-highest-ranking Serb official in the -- in the Serbian [as interpreted] MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you saw him in an office where he was with Bruno Stojic, the representative of the Croatian Democratic Union, and Hilmo Selimovic, representative of the SDA; they were both high-ranking officials of the MUP of the Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I'm informed that there is a mistake in the transcript. Page 21, line 22, it says Serbian MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I was speaking about the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when you came there to complain, Mr. Mandic and the other two were making jokes about you; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, you are not the only professional police officer who fared this way after the victory of the ethnic parties and got inappropriate treatment; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, in 2006, you were a member of the Parliamentary Commission of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina for investigating crimes committed against the citizens of Sarajevo during the war. You said that during the interview, but I believe Mr. Hannis didn't ask you questions about that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, your mother-in-law also disappeared in 1992 in Sarajevo ; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And she's still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember your testimony correctly, in late June, throughout August, and onto September, and certainly even later, you tried to find out through private channels what was happening to your mother-in-law in Sarajevo but you were unable to get any information; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made many attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, even today you don't know what happened to her, nor have you been able to get any information; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only make conjectures. I don't know enough. What I do know is insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Such cases of people, that is, civilians going missing in Sarajevo in 1992 and later on, were not rare; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only in the neighbourhood where I lived five Serb houses were left empty, that is round the place where mother-in-law lived, and these people are still missing. I can give you their names, in case anybody doubts my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not opposed to that. I don't know how relevant it is to this case. But maybe you can mention their names.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mila Saratlija, Mara Saratlija, the Mijanovic married couple, and my mother-in-law. They were all taken away on -- the same way and are missing still.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about mid-1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was late July. We -- that's more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will take you back to the situation in 1992 [as interpreted], late 1992, because I think it's relevant to this case. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I said 1991, and 1992 is recorded. So let's go back to late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On which day were you appointed to your new post in Marin Dvor, and what kind of a position was that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I was transferred on the 1st of June, and the decision bore the date of a few days earlier, so I cannot be very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, since June 1991, all the way through mid-September, there were no particular problems in your work; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I can see from some statements of yours that as of the 18th of September, when you were taking your family to the seaside, and that's why you remember the exact date, the situation changed; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you returned, you were told that the reserve police force had been mobilized and that over 95 per cent of the weapons belonging to the police had been given, or handed out, to Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you expressed your concern, that is, the concern of Serb police officers, you expressed your concerns to Rusdo Kuhinja, the chief of the police station of Marin Dvor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood correctly, he tried to persuade you that 95 per cent of the reserve police that were mobilized were Muslims and that they received weapons. He tried to persuade you that wasn't true; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To check that, you and your deputy, Muhamed Agic, who was also a Muslim, you went to visit some of these reserve police stations; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And once you had visited those police stations, if I understood correctly, you found four reserve police stations which had almost exclusively a Muslim staff; they were armed and mobilized?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Agic accompanied me only to two such stations, and I visited two on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But there were four stations that had almost exclusively Muslim staff; right? I mean, reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almost 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 24 of the transcript, in line 10, it said -- it says, or it was recorded -- actually, I was saying that your chief Rusdo Kuhinja tried to persuade you that it wasn't true that 95 per cent of the reserve police that were mobilized were Muslims and that they received rifles. It was recorded otherwise in the transcript, hence my intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You had also information that one Skrijelj, about whom you had intelligence that he was engaging in smuggling weapons, was the one who distributed those weapons to reserve police officers from official police warehouses; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can provide explanation to make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Centar had --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do slow down.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That municipality where I was had two police stations and one public security station, because, mind you, one public security can include several stations. At Bjelave, the second police station that belonged to the public security station of Centar, the -- most police officers were Muslims, and that reflected the composition of the population. That man Skrijelj, that was his family name, he was a target of a search of the -- by the members of the city SUP because he was suspected to be involved in smuggling weapons some two or three months before this distribution of weapons took place. So that man Skrijelj entered the police station at Bjelave and he distributed weapons as he thought fit. For those weapons, I had no information who had received them; whereas, for the Marin Dvor station, I did have all lists. I wanted to add that to make it clearer so that there be no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these irregularities, to use this euphemism, are something you informed the MUP about; namely, the minister and Deputy Zepinic and probably Momo Mandic, as Assistant Minister for the police, as well as the chief of Centar, Mr. Sabovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may add something that was of particular concern in this case, which was that in the list of people who were issued with weapons in Marin Dvor, I found 32 persons who had either been held responsible or criminal reports were filed against them for committing acts which are incompatible with the job of police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But to move on, the essence is that there was no feedback from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to your letter; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then after a certain passage of time, a delegation came from the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, and they were accompanied by some senior people from the centre, and also from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, once again, you informed them about the situation; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, do you know that the Hadzici SJB, which is one of the municipalities within Sarajevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the urban municipalities belonging to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this SJB provided physical security to the MUP facilities in Rakovica, which were weapons depots. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each station covered the facilities in their territory, facilities of importance, such as depots and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the territory of that SJB, the Hadzici SJB, there were several cases of similar abuse where the weapons from the police depots were distributed without authorisation to the Muslims in late 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the meeting that I described, the meeting which I think took place in Ilidza at the Hotel Bosnia or Hotel Serbia, Glavas, Tiho - I think that he was the commander of the station in Hadzici - spoke about the problems which were of a similar nature as the problems that I encountered at Marin Dvor, concerning weapons, distribution of weapons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just add: It just came to me that I did not mention this man earlier. And when you started talking about the subject, his name popped up in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these cases of distribution of weapons and transfer into reserve police force of persons who did not get security clearance, there were also problems with personnel in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, other problems; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that some persons who, based on their way of life and their qualities, were appointed to leading positions in the police, despite the fact that their -- they had no adequate qualities?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this was particularly widespread among the Muslim community, as far as you know; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It took place in the area where I was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not quite sure whether it's time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... We've got four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the last topic before the break. I think that in one of your statements - and you testified in the case of Lalovic et al. before the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina - you spoke about how you learned about being put on the elimination list, on the list of people to be eliminated. Could you please explain briefly what sort of a list it was, and how did you learn about your name on that list?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, due to everything that went on, and there were a number of things going on, the situation escalated from the point where they were just issuing warnings to the point where a friend of mine - and this was sometime in October - and I knew her because I had sent her family to Germany early on, so she called me on the phone and asked to meet with me urgently. I had a young child and I also had guests in my house and I didn't feel like going out, so I asked if that could wait. And since this friend of mine insisted, I asked her to come to my apartment and she did. In a brief conversation, she told me, Beware, you are a target. And initially I didn't quite understand what she was aiming at, until she took out a list. It was just a plain sheet of paper with a list, written in -- written with a pen, and out of seven people, my name was one of them. She told me that this list was read out in Stari Grad SJB, and then the list was simply copied down. And this was the list of people who had to be eliminated. Until then, I didn't really take this seriously. I thought that everybody had the same frame of mind as I did, and I never thought that peoples' lives were worthless. This was the first time I realised that I was at risk, and in two days I put my wife and our eight-month-old child on a plane to Hamburg. And this is what I can tell you in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just two things that need to be clarified: When you say October, you're referring to October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family left for Hamburg on the 11th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the information that you received is something that you received on the 8th or 9th of October; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. This was 20 days after the mobilisation and everything that was going on, and throughout that time I was advocating lawfulness in work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, and the lady who brought you that document, who brought you the list of the persons to be eliminated, was actually the elimination that was supposed to take place, should certain events occur?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the list of people that were to be eliminated first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to you -- you said that there was a total of seven persons on that list. In addition to you, were the other six also Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were Serbs and members of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: The chief of the Stari Grad station was Ismet Dahic; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was Ismet or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the other name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that it was Ismet, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, both Ismet Dahic and Bezdrob, Enes, were Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And one of them, at that point in time, was the chief of the Stari Grad station; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one brief thing before the witness comes in. We have seen that a formal motion has been announced for the stipulated facts. I think ... I think we -- we made it clear on Friday that no formal motion is needed. We have -- we have now those -- the facts that you -- that are already stipulated, and that's okay. We have your signed notice on that, so there is no further problem. The only thing that we -- we are still awaiting for, the follow-up of the other -- the discussions over the weekend. But that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. It's obvious that probably we, as well as our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, misunderstood your instruction, because we -- it was my understanding that, for the already stipulated facts, that we are supposed to send an e-mail with a signature, as a notice. But for the -- for the ones that we were discussing over the last three, four days, that we would need to file a joint motion. That is -- that was my understanding. I might be wrong, so whatever the Trial Chamber is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As long -- as long as we know what happens, it's in the parties' hands to stipulate, so if we are -- if we get normal notice of the fact of what is stipulated, it's okay with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. We will discuss with our friends from the Prosecution. And, of course, what -- what we are doing is precisely that the Trial Chamber should -- should be aware of. That goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Planojevic, I just wanted to bring to your attention that in terms of the matter that you raised when we began this afternoon that we have observed that the article in question has since been removed from the web site of SENSE. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, since we established that your experience as an active-duty policeman spans over 30 years, perhaps you can tell me something about the check-points at which ID checks were carried out, as well as vehicle control, in terms of security measures, and it pertained to all vehicular traffic. Such exercises were conducted in the former Yugoslavia as a type of operational measures undertaken by the police?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were tactical operational measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Such tactical operational measures as setting up check-points was standard practice when erected along access routes to towns or at important intersections of regional roads; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Such operational tactical measures, namely, the establishing of the check-points, is something that was pursued throughout the former Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia even before 1994 [as interpreted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had always been done, ever since I began working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 32, line 20, I think it says "1994," whereas I believe I said "1990."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Especially after the events of 1990 and 1991, such operational tactical measures became much more frequent, in terms of the number of check-points that were set up throughout the SFRY; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Including Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with an operation jointly carried out in 1992 by the ministry of the socialist republic -- the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the federal SUP called Punkt 1991. Or perhaps it was the JNA; I'm not certain. Are you familiar with the operation?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were both. In agreement with the minister, they arrived in the location where I represented the federal ministry. And there were representatives of the B&H MUP there. On the other hand, there was the agreement between Kukanjac, as the army commander, and Minister Delimustafic, I believe, to have joint patrols because there were raising tensions at the time. I believe this is how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to the check-points which were set up as a result of the agreement between the Ministry of Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the federal SUP, there were also joint check-points manned by military policemen and civilian policemen pursuant to another agreement between the commander of the 2nd Military District, General Kukanjac, and the interior minister of B&H, Alija Delimustafic. Is that the gist of your answer?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Another routine operational measure in police work is to ascertain the identity of persons by checking their IDs or other personal documents.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a operational measure to put in place, that would be the first step to take, which would then be followed by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 1989 and the period up to 1992, the -- there was an increasing problem of illegal smuggling of arms, hence, one of regular operational measures undertaken at such check-points was also to check the trunks of motor vehicles as well as any luggage found therein; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On Friday, you briefly discussed a topic with Mr. Hannis, namely, the event of the 4th of April in the evening. I would simply like to briefly enumerate all the things that took place on the 4th of April. It is a fact that on the 4th of April, in the evening, your workmate Risticovic [phoen] from the town SUP was attacked in the public security station?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction: It was the town SUP, meaning that the unit covered the whole town. He was an employee of the town SUP. And at the very entrance of the building, he was badly beaten up and left unconscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It took place on the 4th of April in the evening?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was attacked and beaten up by members of the Green Beret; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that when I went to visit him. He was in hospital for quite a long time. It was the makeshift hospital that we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the Green Berets put the barrel of a gun in his mouth, pulling the trigger, but the chamber was actually empty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he believes that the gun actually misfired, not that the chamber had been empty. He was simply lucky enough, but he still feels the consequences of that shock. He never fully recovered. I believe he resides in the Netherlands now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is also true that your workmate Lazar Bojanic was also beaten up that evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if you need any further explanations, I'm ready to offer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was also a member of the police and was on duty when he was beaten up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was, yes. He was the shift leader in the Novo Sarajevo Police Station. Therefore, yes, he was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, he saw Ismet Dahic accompanied by Mr. Puskar, who was at the helm of the Green Berets, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was some 150 or 200 metres away from the Novo Sarajevo Police Station. He went there to assist the station, which had been attacked, and he received a blow to the head with a butt rifle -- with a rifle butt, and he asked the man you mentioned to allow him to go to the nearest emergency ward to receive assistance, and was allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When Lazar Bojanic was attacked, another Serb police member was killed. I believe his first name was Pero. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Petrovic was killed. He was not an employee of that particular station. He just happened to be there because he came to report a crime. He was there by chance. First, he received a blow with a rifle butt and was then shot at the back of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it all took place inside the Novo Sarajevo Police Station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room of the shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You -- we mentioned Ismet Dahic, who was a career policeman and either the chief or commander of the SJB in Stari Grad in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We attended high school together, and our careers developed in a similar fashion. We had always worked for the police. I -- he used to be the chief there, but at the moment when I received that document, I don't remember whether he was any longer in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since he was near the Novo Sarajevo Police Station accompanied by Sakib Puskar, who was the leader of the Green Berets, he was there in an area which was not under the competence of his public security station.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was another police station between the two. That was the approximate distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A certain Slobodan Vreco also had a number of hooded men enter his SJB on the night of the 4th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, Slobodan Vreco was in front of the Novo Sarajevo Police Station when they stormed the premises and he fled. He wasn't in the building itself and was not affected by the attack. He simply escaped before it all took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That same evening, in your station, where you were on duty, a person was brought in, as you described, whereupon you learned that the person had been armed and had been ordered to guard the municipal assembly building. Given that it made you conclude that there was something going on, you went home.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And everything we have just been discussing, these incidents, is something you were informed of by telephone that evening, as they transpired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the information I received that evening; whereas, other information I received in contact with the witnesses, the participants of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What you were able to conclude, and it is why you left the station in Marin Dvor to go home, is something that amounted to a sychronised attack on most SJBs in Sarajevo territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I can clarify further. The Serb police in Stari Grad left the area a month before the war, so there was a police station with only one Serb policeman; I believe his name was Tosic. The other policeman arrived in the centre, where I was, there were four of them, because of the pressure that had been put on them. The ethnic make-up in -- of the population in Stari Grad is some 70 per cent of Muslims. Marin Dvor, which is the next station, and Bjelave, were in the territory that had already been abandoned by most Serbs. And that evening, as I said, I asked that station commander to keep them there until the next morning. So in the centre there were nearly 400 beret members in action. There was the police hall in the area of the town centre which was also taken over by Jusuf Prazina, a hardened criminal. And there was a number of other stations that were taken over as well. The same goes for the traffic police. They were close to the Novo Sarajevo station. I already told you about the Novo Sarajevo station. As for the Novi Grad SJB, when I called them that evening, I learned that they had two Serbs in that shift. So it was only Ilidza that was left. And there were some 60 to 70 per cent of Serbs living in Ilidza. And that station had a Bosniak chief, Edin Milic [phoen]. He appeared on TV in mid-April. I believe his name was Edin Mlijevic [phoen]. That was more or less the sequence. Those stations were taken over during that night. It wasn't that we left because we wanted to; our lives were at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also received some threats on the phone that night. You spoke about that already. There's no doubt that you and other Serb police officers were scared for yourselves and for your families; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But most of us had already taken our families out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Planojevic, the events on the 4th of April were really a -- crossing the point of no return; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to be blind not to notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the following day, with a group of colleagues, you went to Vraca. And you said on Friday, giving evidence to Mr. Hannis, that it had been agreed that Vraca should be the headquarters of the SUP of the Republika Srpska. That's why it wasn't expected that there would be a conflict. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, upon your departure on the 5th, in the afternoon hours, a conflict did break out; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope that you know that the agreement about the division of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of the Cutileiro Plan; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said as much on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On Friday, you stated that upon leaving Vraca on the 5th in the morning, you first went to Pionirska and then to Rogatica, I think, and that you reported for duty at the MUP on Monday. You said it was the 19th of April. But I checked, as -- Monday was the 20th of April. Do you remember it was a Monday?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly was Monday. I thought it was the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were appointed assistant minister, and you got an office at the school at Vraca; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, your immediate superior was the under-secretary for public security, Mr. Cedo Kljajic, since the administration you headed belonged to public security; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was chief of police and the crime services.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with my conclusion that the MUP of the RS was being created in April from scratch; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we called it building it from a -- from a tree stump.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that when you reported for duty you didn't even have typewriters; right? Or at least not enough.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More of us shared one. That was the police school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, the shortage of personnel was a huge problem. I mean, personnel of the MUP of the RS at the time. Right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our ranks were sparse because many of us had left to see their families at their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, there was a chaotic situation, and if I understood correctly, most people first took their families to a safe place, and that was their first priority, rather than doing their job; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at the time when you arrived and during the following period that you spent at Vraca, that is, about a month and a half, you had no communication with any CSB, did you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most of them still weren't in existence. They hadn't yet been established or up and running. When I say that, I mean they existed on paper, but there was no infrastructure in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that even the Law on the Interior of the RS from March 1992 envisages the CSB of Ugljevik as one of the CSBs and -- rather than Bijeljina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were no conditions. I don't think I need explain. But the law said Bijeljina. But there was never one man there, so it couldn't -- it couldn't function.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 40, line 25, the law said Ugljevik, but that was a mistake. Later the law had to be amended to -- to say Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood your evidence given on Friday correctly, on the 25th of April you arrived at Vraca, and you stayed there until the 8th of May, when you went to Belgrade because your wife had given birth to a child?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in the meantime, I also went there and spent three days there for Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then you returned on or about 27th of May to Vraca. And then between the 5th and 7th of June, 1992, you were transferred to Kalovita Brda, that is, the building at Pale?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I'm not certain about the dates. It may be a day or two earlier or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In June, you went to some municipalities in the territory of Sarajevo: Vogosca, Ilidza, Ilijas. Right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On 9 July, did you go to Belgrade to attend the first collegium which was held on the 11th, and did you return from that collegium on or about the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a correction. I went there on the 9th of June and spent seven days there. And then did I go there in July. I remember the date because of the funerals and the -- the fighting on the 8th. Once the fighting stopped, I -- on the following day, I immediately went to Belgrade and stayed there seven days, or eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, it's a fact that on or about 9 July you went to Belgrade and returned about the 19th. And then on the 21st or 22nd of July, you were relieved of your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In July, the shortage of materiel and equipment, shortcomings in communications lines, shortage of personnel in the MUP of the RS were all acute problems; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, practically throughout the war, but especially during that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1419.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I'll ask you to comment. While we're waiting, I see that your answer -- or, yes, it has been recorded. I apologise. Sir, this is a list of employees of the MUP headquarters for July 1992. It says: MUP headquarters collegium. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this because at one moment, even today, you commented on two persons, and that is Zoran Jasarevic, number 10; it says driver of the minister or the ministry. And number 14, Goran Abazovic, escort. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are these the persons you said accompanied Minister Mico Stanisic in July 1992? One was his driver, and the other his escort.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On Friday, document 1D46 was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document? It's dated 15 May 1992. Do you remember seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your evidence was that -- on Friday, that on 15 May you were not at Vraca but in Belgrade. However, you were pretty certain that Cedo Kljajic familiarized with you the contents of this document. Do you remember saying that on Friday?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the contents of the document; that's true. But I'm not sure whether I saw the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my examination, we mentioned the mobilisation of the reserve force of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in September 1991, that is, when we were discussing that and the -- the arming of the reserve force. Now tell me about this mobilisation and this arming process. This -- was this in line with the defence plans of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. But every station had its own plans and everything was prescribed in these station-level plans, not only at the level of the republic. Because each station had to develop its plans, and it had to be ready to act upon them. Especially in wartime, this meant the implementation of all the laws upon which these plans were founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is a fact, isn't it, that according to the then-laws, the laws in force then, and specifically the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, which was both at the republic level and at the federal level, each organ, each institution, and each company had to have a plan for wartime organisation; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As you have testified, let me just summarise that. Such a plan on wartime organisation existed at the level of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also at the level of all CSBs, and, finally, at the level of each individual SJB in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To go back now to this document dated the 15th of May. Mr. Planojevic, it is a fact, isn't it, and you testified about it, that you never ever issued an order as a member of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I formulated the question erroneously, so it's not entirely clear. Therefore, it's true that you never ever issued an order as a member of the staff; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
